title: The power of three
settingKo: 연설 코치가 세 가지로 묶어 말하는 기법을 가르칩니다.

lines.text: Notice how memorable phrases come in threes: veni, vidi, vici, or government of the people, by the people, for the people.
lines.ko: 기억에 남는 문구는 셋으로 와요. 왔노라 보았노라 이겼노라, 또는 국민의, 국민에 의한, 국민을 위한.

lines.text: Is there a reason three works better than two or four?
lines.ko: 둘이나 넷보다 셋이 더 잘 통하는 이유가 있나요?

lines.text: Two feels like a comparison, four feels like a list, but three feels complete, like a beginning, a middle, and an end.
lines.ko: 둘은 비교 같고 넷은 목록 같지만 셋은 시작, 중간, 끝처럼 완결된 느낌을 줘요.

lines.text: So instead of saying our product is fast, I should say it's fast, simple, and reliable.
lines.ko: 그럼 제품이 빠르다고만 하지 말고 빠르고, 간단하고, 믿을 수 있다고 해야겠네요.

response.situationKo: 자기 자신이나 팀을 세 단어로 소개해 보세요.
response.prompt: Describe your team in exactly three words, then explain.

answers.text: Curious, honest, and stubborn. We ask questions, say what we think, and don't give up.
answers.noteKo: 세 단어 뒤에 세 가지 설명을 붙였어요.

answers.text: Small, fast, and fearless, because we ship every week and learn from every mistake.
Thoughtful, reliable, and kind. In that order, and always together.
Loud, caffeinated, brilliant. Mostly in that order.

title: Repeating for rhythm
settingKo: 같은 말을 문장 처음에 반복하는 기법을 연습합니다.

lines.text: Repetition at the start of sentences builds momentum. Listen: we will listen, we will learn, we will do better.
lines.ko: 문장 처음의 반복은 추진력을 만들어요. 들어 봐요: 우리는 듣고, 배우고, 더 잘할 겁니다.

lines.text: It sounds powerful, but couldn't it also sound repetitive and boring?
lines.ko: 힘 있게 들리는데 반복적이고 지루하게 들릴 수도 있지 않나요?

lines.text: Only if you overuse it. Save it for the moment you want the audience to feel something, usually near the end.
lines.ko: 남용하면 그래요. 청중이 뭔가를 느끼길 원하는 순간, 보통 끝 무렵에 아껴 쓰세요.

lines.text: Then I'll use it once, in my closing, and keep the rest of the speech plain.
lines.ko: 그럼 마무리에서 한 번만 쓰고 나머지는 담백하게 할게요.

options: 청중이 감정을 느끼길 원하는 마지막 즈음에

response.situationKo: 같은 구절을 세 번 반복하는 짧은 마무리 문장을 만들어 보세요.
response.prompt: Give me a closing line using repetition.

answers.text: For every customer we lost, for every bug we shipped, for every promise we broke, this year we make it right.
We will listen. We will improve. We will earn your trust back.
Not because it's easy, not because it's quick, but because it's right.
answers.noteKo: Not because 반복 후 but으로 전환해요.

answers.text: Together we started, together we struggled, and together we'll finish.

title: Questions that aren't questions
settingKo: 답을 기대하지 않는 질문으로 청중을 사로잡는 법을 배웁니다.

lines.text: Instead of saying 'meetings waste time', ask: how many hours did you spend in meetings last week that changed nothing?
lines.ko: '회의는 시간 낭비'라고 하지 말고 물어보세요. 지난주 아무것도 바꾸지 못한 회의에 몇 시간을 썼나요?

lines.text: Because the audience answers it silently in their own heads.
lines.ko: 청중이 머릿속에서 조용히 답하게 되니까요.

lines.text: Exactly. A statement asks them to agree; a question invites them to discover it themselves.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 진술은 동의를 요구하고, 질문은 스스로 발견하도록 초대해요.

lines.text: But if I ask too many, I'll sound like a game-show host.
lines.ko: 그래도 너무 많이 물으면 퀴즈쇼 진행자처럼 들릴 거예요.

phrases.en: A question invites them to discover it themselves.

response.situationKo: 주장을 수사 의문문으로 바꿔서 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Turn 'we should recycle more' into a rhetorical question.

answers.text: How many of the bottles you threw away this year are still sitting in a landfill?
Would you throw your rubbish into your own garden? Then why into the ocean?
What kind of world are we leaving for the children who will clean up after us?
Who actually enjoys paying for more bin bags every week?

title: Opposites side by side
settingKo: 반대되는 개념을 나란히 놓아 메시지를 선명하게 하는 법을 배웁니다.

lines.text: Antithesis places opposites side by side. Neil Armstrong: one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
lines.ko: 대조법은 반대를 나란히 놓아요. 닐 암스트롱: 한 사람에게는 작은 한 걸음, 인류에게는 거대한 도약.

lines.text: Small and giant, man and mankind. The contrast makes both halves stronger.
lines.ko: 작은 것과 거대한 것, 한 사람과 인류. 대조가 양쪽을 더 강하게 만드네요.

lines.text: Try it with your pitch. What's the opposite of what your competitors promise?
lines.ko: 피치에 써 봐요. 경쟁사가 약속하는 것의 반대는 뭐죠?

lines.text: They promise more features; we promise fewer headaches.
lines.ko: 그들은 더 많은 기능을, 우리는 더 적은 골칫거리를 약속해요.

phrases.en: One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
phrases.ko: 한 사람에게는 작은 걸음, 인류에게는 거대한 도약.

phrases.en: The contrast makes both halves stronger.

response.situationKo: 대조법으로 자신의 신념이나 원칙을 한 문장으로 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Give me your philosophy in one contrasting sentence.

answers.text: Success isn't about working longer, it's about working on the right things.
answers.noteKo: not about A, it's about B 구조예요.

answers.text: Speak less, listen more.
We don't sell software; we sell back people's evenings.
Fewer meetings, better decisions. Simple as that.

title: Explaining with analogies
settingKo: 어려운 개념을 일상적인 비유로 설명하는 연습을 합니다.

lines.text: Explain compound interest to someone who's never heard of it, without using a single number.
lines.ko: 숫자 하나 쓰지 말고 복리를 처음 듣는 사람에게 설명해 봐요.

lines.text: It's like a snowball rolling downhill: it picks up snow, gets bigger, and the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.
lines.ko: 언덕을 굴러가는 눈덩이 같아요. 눈을 붙이며 커지고, 커질수록 더 빨리 자라요.

lines.text: Excellent. And what's the lesson hidden in your analogy?
lines.ko: 훌륭해요. 그 비유에 숨은 교훈은 뭐예요?

lines.text: Start the snowball early, because the hill doesn't get any longer.
lines.ko: 눈덩이를 일찍 굴리기 시작하라는 거죠. 언덕은 더 길어지지 않으니까요.

phrases.en: It's like a snowball rolling downhill.
The hill doesn't get any longer.

response.situationKo: 어려운 개념 하나를 일상적인 비유로 설명해 보세요.
response.prompt: Explain what a firewall does, using an analogy.

answers.text: It's like a bouncer at a club door, checking everyone's ID and turning away anyone suspicious.
Think of it as the security desk in an office building, deciding who gets in and who doesn't.
Imagine a filter on a tap: water goes through, but the dirt stays out.
Basically, it's your computer's very grumpy doorman.

title: Ethos, pathos, logos
settingKo: 아리스토텔레스의 설득 세 요소로 자기 발표를 분석합니다.

lines.text: Aristotle said persuasion rests on three things: your credibility, the audience's emotions, and logical argument.
lines.ko: 아리스토텔레스는 설득이 세 가지에 기댄다고 했어요. 신뢰성, 청중의 감정, 논리적 주장.

lines.text: My presentation is full of data, so I'm strong on logic, but I suspect it's emotionally flat.
lines.ko: 제 발표는 데이터로 가득해서 논리는 강한데 감정적으로는 밋밋한 것 같아요.

lines.text: Then open with one real customer's story before you show a single chart.
lines.ko: 그럼 그래프를 하나라도 보여 주기 전에 실제 고객 한 명의 이야기로 시작해요.

lines.text: And mention my ten years in the industry early, so they trust the numbers that follow.
lines.ko: 그리고 업계 10년 경력을 초반에 말해서 뒤에 나오는 숫자를 믿게 하죠.

phrases.en: So they trust the numbers that follow.

response.situationKo: 신뢰, 감정, 논리를 모두 담아 짧게 설득해 보세요.
response.prompt: Convince us to fund the after-school reading program.

answers.text: As a teacher for fifteen years, I've seen it work. Last year, Maya read her first full book. And for every dollar, we see a measurable gain in test scores.
Imagine being ten and unable to read a menu. The data shows our program fixes that in one year, for less than a school trip costs.
I've run this program for six years. Here's one story and three numbers.
One kid, one book, one year. That's the pitch, and here's the proof.

title: Admit, then argue
settingKo: 토론에서 상대 논점을 먼저 인정하고 반박하는 법을 배웁니다.

lines.text: The strongest debaters concede the opponent's best point before turning it around.
lines.ko: 가장 강한 토론자는 상대의 최고 논점을 먼저 인정하고 뒤집어요.

lines.text: Doesn't admitting their point make me look weaker?
lines.ko: 상대 논점을 인정하면 제가 약해 보이지 않나요?

lines.text: The opposite. It shows you've listened, and it makes your rebuttal sound fair rather than defensive.
lines.ko: 반대예요. 들었다는 걸 보여 주고 반박이 방어적이지 않고 공정하게 들리게 해요.

lines.text: So: it's true that the policy costs more upfront, but it saves twice as much within five years.
lines.ko: 그러니까: 그 정책이 초기 비용은 더 드는 게 사실이지만 5년 안에 두 배를 절약한다.

phrases.en: Concede the best point before turning it around.

response.situationKo: 상대의 좋은 논점을 인정한 뒤 반박해 보세요.
response.prompt: Opponent: Remote work isolates people and weakens company culture.

answers.text: It's true that isolation is a real risk. However, the solution is better rituals, not more commuting.
I'd agree culture can suffer. That said, many remote teams report stronger trust because work is judged by results.
Fair point, but offices didn't guarantee culture either. Plenty of people felt invisible at their desks.
Totally, loneliness is real. But so is a two-hour commute.

title: The opening hook
settingKo: 발표의 첫 문장을 더 강렬하게 바꾸는 연습을 합니다.

lines.text: My talk starts with, 'Hello, my name is Min, and today I'll talk about sleep.'
lines.ko: 제 발표는 '안녕하세요, 저는 민이고 오늘은 잠에 대해 이야기하겠습니다'로 시작해요.

lines.text: That's polite, but nobody will remember it. Start with a surprising fact or a tiny story instead.
lines.ko: 예의 바르지만 아무도 기억 못 해요. 대신 놀라운 사실이나 짧은 이야기로 시작해요.

lines.text: How about: 'Last night, a third of this room slept less than six hours, and most of you don't even know it.'
lines.ko: 이건 어때요: '어젯밤 이 방의 3분의 1은 6시간도 못 잤고 대부분은 그걸 모릅니다.'

lines.text: Much better. Now they're curious, and you can introduce yourself after you've earned their attention.
lines.ko: 훨씬 나아요. 이제 궁금해하니까 관심을 얻은 뒤에 자기소개를 하면 돼요.

response.situationKo: 아래 주제로 청중을 사로잡는 첫 문장을 만들어 보세요.
response.prompt: Your topic is food waste. Give me your first sentence.

answers.text: Right now, somewhere in this city, a truck is dumping enough good food to feed a school.
Imagine buying three bags of groceries, then throwing one in the bin on the way home. That's what we do every week.
Did you know that a third of all food produced in the world is never eaten?
Raise your hand if you've ever found something furry in the back of your fridge.

title: Ending with a call to action
settingKo: 발표 마무리를 구체적인 행동 요청으로 바꿉니다.

lines.text: I end my talk with, 'So, yeah, that's it. Thanks.' It feels a bit weak.
lines.ko: 발표를 '그래서, 네, 끝이에요. 감사합니다'로 끝내는데 좀 약한 것 같아요.

lines.text: It is. Ask for one specific action they can take this week, not a vague hope.
lines.ko: 약해요. 막연한 바람 말고 이번 주에 할 수 있는 구체적인 행동 하나를 요청해요.

lines.text: So instead of 'please sleep more', I could say 'tonight, put your phone outside the bedroom'.
lines.ko: 그럼 '잠을 더 자세요' 대신 '오늘 밤 휴대폰을 침실 밖에 두세요'라고 하면 되겠네요.

lines.text: Exactly. Small, specific, and tonight. That's what people actually remember and do.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 작고, 구체적이고, 오늘 밤. 사람들이 실제로 기억하고 행동하는 거예요.

response.situationKo: 아래 주제로 구체적인 행동 요청으로 발표를 마무리해 보세요.
response.prompt: Close your talk on saving money.

answers.text: Before you leave this room, open your banking app and set up one automatic transfer, however small.
This week, cancel one subscription you forgot you had. That's it. Just one.
Tonight, write down every purchase you made today. You'll be surprised.
One thing: next coffee, make it at home. Your future self will send a thank-you note.

title: Not bad at all
settingKo: 부정을 부정해 강조하는 영어식 완곡 표현을 배웁니다.

lines.text: When an English speaker says 'not bad', they often mean 'pretty good', and 'not unpleasant' can mean 'quite nice'.
lines.ko: 영어 화자가 'not bad'라고 하면 보통 '꽤 좋다'는 뜻이고, 'not unpleasant'는 '꽤 괜찮다'일 수 있어요.

lines.text: Why not just say it directly?
lines.ko: 왜 그냥 직접 말하지 않아요?

lines.text: It sounds modest and a little dry, especially in British English. 'It was no small achievement' is warmer than 'it was big'.
lines.ko: 겸손하고 약간 건조하게 들려서요. 특히 영국 영어에서요. '작은 성과가 아니었다'가 '컸다'보다 따뜻해요.

lines.text: So when my boss said my report was 'not without merit', was that praise or criticism?
lines.ko: 그럼 상사가 제 보고서가 '장점이 없지 않다'고 한 건 칭찬이에요, 비판이에요?

response.situationKo: 완곡한 부정 표현(not bad, no small 등)으로 무언가를 칭찬해 보세요.
response.prompt: So, how was the new restaurant?

answers.text: Not bad at all. I'd happily go back.
answers.noteKo: not bad at all은 꽤 좋다는 뜻이에요.

answers.text: Not half bad, actually. The desserts were a highlight.
Getting a table on a Saturday was no small feat, and the food justified it.
answers.noteKo: no small feat는 대단한 일이라는 뜻이에요.

answers.text: Honestly, not the worst meal I've had this year.

title: Tomorrow, and tomorrow
settingKo: 영문학 수업에서 맥베스의 유명한 독백을 해석합니다.

lines.text: Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace from day to day. What's Macbeth feeling here?
lines.ko: 내일, 그리고 내일, 그리고 내일이 하루하루 이 하찮은 걸음으로 기어간다. 맥베스는 여기서 어떤 감정일까요?

lines.text: Exhaustion, maybe despair. The repetition makes time feel endless and pointless.
lines.ko: 지침, 어쩌면 절망이요. 반복이 시간을 끝없고 무의미하게 느끼게 해요.

lines.text: Good. He's just heard his wife is dead, and suddenly all his ambition looks meaningless.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 그는 방금 아내의 죽음을 들었고, 갑자기 모든 야망이 의미 없어 보이죠.

lines.text: So the slow rhythm of the words actually imitates the slowness he's describing.
lines.ko: 그럼 단어의 느린 리듬이 그가 묘사하는 느림을 실제로 흉내 내는 거네요.

response.situationKo: 문학 작품의 한 구절이 왜 효과적인지 분석해 보세요.
response.prompt: Why do you think this line has lasted four hundred years?

answers.text: Because everyone has felt that heavy, endless kind of tiredness at some point.
The repetition does the work. You feel the days dragging before you even understand the words.
It captures a universal feeling in very simple language, which is surprisingly rare.
Honestly? Mondays. It's basically a poem about Mondays.

title: What's in a name?
settingKo: 친구와 줄리엣의 유명한 대사를 브랜드 이름 문제에 빗대어 이야기합니다.

lines.text: We've spent three weeks arguing about the company name. Honestly, what's in a name?
lines.ko: 회사 이름 때문에 3주째 싸우고 있어. 솔직히 이름이 뭐가 중요해?

lines.text: That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. Juliet would agree with you.
lines.ko: 장미를 다른 이름으로 불러도 똑같이 향기로울 거야. 줄리엣이 네 편이겠네.

lines.text: Exactly. The product matters, not the label.
lines.ko: 바로 그거야. 중요한 건 이름표가 아니라 제품이지.

lines.text: Mind you, the name caused her quite a lot of trouble in the end, so maybe it matters more than she thought.
lines.ko: 그런데 결국 그 이름 때문에 그녀가 꽤 큰 곤경에 빠졌잖아. 생각보다 이름이 중요할지도 몰라.

gist.questionKo: 두 번째 사람의 마지막 말의 의미는?

phrases.en: A rose by any other name would smell as sweet.
phrases.ko: 장미는 다른 이름으로 불러도 똑같이 향기롭다.

response.situationKo: 이름(브랜드)이 중요한지에 대해 명구절을 활용해 의견을 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Does a good name really matter for a product?

answers.text: Juliet said a rose would smell as sweet, but nobody buys a rose they can't remember the name of.
I'd argue it matters for first impressions, but after that, the product does the talking.
A memorable name gets you through the door. Quality keeps you in the room.
Matters a bit. Call your app 'Sadness Calculator' and see how it goes.

title: Friends, Romans, countrymen
settingKo: 줄리어스 시저의 안토니우스 연설에서 반어적 설득 기법을 분석합니다.

lines.text: Antony keeps calling Brutus 'an honourable man', but each time, the audience believes it a little less.
lines.ko: 안토니우스는 브루투스를 계속 '고결한 사람'이라고 부르는데, 매번 청중은 조금씩 덜 믿게 돼요.

lines.text: So he's praising Brutus on the surface while destroying him underneath.
lines.ko: 그러니까 겉으로는 브루투스를 칭찬하면서 속으로는 무너뜨리는 거네요.

lines.text: Exactly. He also says 'I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him', and then praises him for the rest of the speech.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 또 '시저를 칭찬하러 온 게 아니라 묻으러 왔다'고 하고는 연설 내내 칭찬하죠.

lines.text: It's brilliant manipulation. He never says 'turn against Brutus', yet that's exactly what the crowd does.
lines.ko: 탁월한 조종이네요. '브루투스에게 등 돌려라'고 한 번도 말하지 않는데 군중은 정확히 그렇게 하죠.

phrases.en: I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.
phrases.ko: 시저를 칭찬하러 온 게 아니라 묻으러 왔다. (셰익스피어 '줄리어스 시저')

response.situationKo: 말한 것과 실제 의도가 다른(반어적) 표현의 예를 들어 설명해 보세요.
response.prompt: Can you think of a modern example of saying one thing and meaning another?

answers.text: When someone says 'with all due respect' in a meeting, it usually means they're about to disagree strongly.
For example, 'I'm sure you had your reasons' often means 'I think you were wrong'.
A politician saying 'I have great respect for my opponent' right before attacking their record.
My mum saying 'do whatever you want'. It absolutely does not mean that.

title: Brevity is the soul of wit
settingKo: 장황한 보고서를 쓴 동료에게 햄릿의 대사로 조언합니다.

lines.text: My summary is eleven pages. Is that too long for the leadership team?
lines.ko: 제 요약이 11쪽이에요. 경영진한테 너무 길까요?

lines.text: Polonius says brevity is the soul of wit, which is funny, because he's the most long-winded character in Hamlet.
lines.ko: 폴로니어스가 간결함이 재치의 영혼이라고 하는데, 웃기게도 그가 햄릿에서 가장 장황한 인물이에요.

lines.text: So I'm being Polonius. What would you cut?
lines.ko: 그럼 제가 폴로니어스네요. 뭘 빼시겠어요?

lines.text: Keep one page: the decision you need, the three reasons, and the risk. Put everything else in an appendix.
lines.ko: 한 쪽만 남겨요. 필요한 결정, 세 가지 이유, 위험. 나머지는 전부 부록으로.

phrases.en: Brevity is the soul of wit.
Put everything else in an appendix.

response.situationKo: 긴 이야기를 한두 문장으로 요약해 보세요.
response.prompt: In two sentences, what did your team achieve this year?

answers.text: We halved our support response time and doubled customer satisfaction. Next year, we do the same with half the cost.
In short, we rebuilt the checkout, which means fewer lost sales every single day.
We launched in three countries and didn't break anything important. That's the headline.
We fixed what customers complained about most, and they noticed.

title: Bah, humbug!
settingKo: 연말 회식을 싫어하는 동료를 스크루지에 빗대어 농담합니다.

lines.text: You're skipping the holiday party again? Bah, humbug, is it, Mr. Scrooge?
lines.ko: 또 연말 파티 빠져? 쳇, 허튼소리라는 거야, 스크루지 씨?

lines.text: Ha. I'm not against joy, I'm against forced games and a two-hour speech from the CEO.
lines.ko: 하. 난 즐거움에 반대하는 게 아니라 억지 게임이랑 CEO의 두 시간짜리 연설에 반대하는 거야.

lines.text: Fair, but remember Scrooge ends up the happiest man in London once he lets people in.
lines.ko: 그럴 만해. 그래도 스크루지는 사람들에게 마음을 열고 나서 런던에서 가장 행복한 사람이 되잖아.

lines.text: Fine. I'll come for one hour, but if anyone hands me a paper hat, I'm leaving.
lines.ko: 좋아. 한 시간만 갈게. 근데 누가 종이 모자 주면 바로 간다.

response.situationKo: 유명한 문학 캐릭터에 빗대어 친구를 가볍게 놀려 보세요.
response.prompt: My roommate refuses to spend a single cent on anything fun.

answers.text: Sounds like a bit of a Scrooge. Maybe he needs three ghosts to visit him.
He reminds me of Scrooge before the ghosts. Give him time.
Every story needs a Scrooge. Without him, there's no transformation at the end.
If he says 'bah, humbug', you're legally allowed to move out.

title: Lives of quiet desperation
settingKo: 번아웃을 겪는 친구와 소로의 『월든』 구절을 이야기합니다.

lines.text: Thoreau wrote that the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. That line hit me hard this week.
lines.ko: 소로는 대부분의 사람이 조용한 절망의 삶을 산다고 썼어. 이번 주에 그 구절이 크게 와닿았어.

lines.text: He wrote that in the eighteen fifties, and it still sounds like a description of every office I've worked in.
lines.ko: 1850년대에 쓴 건데 아직도 내가 일한 모든 사무실을 묘사하는 것 같아.

lines.text: He went to live in a cabin to find out what he actually needed. I'm not moving to the woods, though.
lines.ko: 그는 진짜 필요한 게 뭔지 알려고 오두막에서 살았지. 그래도 난 숲으로 이사 가진 않을 거야.

lines.text: You don't need the woods. Maybe just one evening a week with no phone and no plans.
lines.ko: 숲까진 필요 없어. 일주일에 하루 저녁만 휴대폰도 계획도 없이 보내 봐.

options: 일주일에 하루 저녁 휴대폰과 계획 없이 지내라

phrases.en: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
phrases.ko: 대부분의 사람은 조용한 절망의 삶을 산다. (소로 '월든')

response.situationKo: 현대인의 삶에 대해 명구절을 인용해 의견을 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Do you think modern life makes people happier or more anxious?

answers.text: Thoreau talked about quiet desperation, and I think phones just made it louder.
We have more choices than ever, but more choices can mean more ways to feel we've chosen wrong.
It depends on whether you use technology or let it use you.
Happier on paper, more anxious at three a.m.

title: A foolish consistency
settingKo: 의견을 바꿨다고 비판받는 동료를 에머슨의 말로 변호합니다.

lines.text: Jake's being attacked for changing his position on the project. People are calling it a flip-flop.
lines.ko: 제이크가 프로젝트에 대한 입장을 바꿨다고 공격받고 있어요. 다들 오락가락한다고 해요.

lines.text: Emerson wrote that a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds. Changing your view with new evidence isn't weakness.
lines.ko: 에머슨은 어리석은 일관성은 좁은 마음의 도깨비라고 했어요. 새 증거로 견해를 바꾸는 건 약함이 아니에요.

lines.text: True, but people want leaders who seem certain.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그래도 사람들은 확신 있어 보이는 리더를 원해요.

lines.text: Then he should explain what changed his mind. Confidence in his reasoning matters more than sticking to his first guess.
lines.ko: 그럼 무엇이 생각을 바꿨는지 설명해야죠. 첫 추측을 고수하는 것보다 추론에 대한 확신이 더 중요해요.

phrases.en: A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.

response.situationKo: 자신이 의견을 바꾼 이유를 설득력 있게 설명해 보세요.
response.prompt: Last month you were against this plan. Why the change?

answers.text: In light of the pilot results, I've changed my mind. The evidence simply outweighed my concerns.
What changed was the data. I'd rather update my view than defend a guess.
I've since spoken to customers, and they described a problem I hadn't understood.
Honestly? I was wrong. Emerson would be proud.

title: The road not taken
settingKo: 진로 고민을 하는 친구와 프로스트의 시를 이야기합니다.

lines.text: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I took the one less traveled by. That's my plan: the risky career.
lines.ko: 숲속에 두 갈래 길이 있었고, 나는 사람들이 덜 간 길을 택했다. 그게 내 계획이야. 위험한 진로.

lines.text: People always quote that as brave advice, but read the whole poem. Frost says both paths were worn about the same.
lines.ko: 다들 그걸 용감한 조언으로 인용하는데 시 전체를 읽어 봐. 프로스트는 두 길이 거의 비슷하게 닳았다고 해.

lines.text: Wait, really? So the choice didn't matter?
lines.ko: 잠깐, 진짜? 그럼 선택이 중요하지 않았다는 거야?

lines.text: More that we tell the story afterwards as if it did. So choose, and then make your choice the right one.
lines.ko: 그보다는 나중에 중요했던 것처럼 이야기를 만든다는 거지. 그러니 고르고, 그 선택을 옳은 것으로 만들어.

options: 선택 후 이야기를 만들어 의미를 부여한다

phrases.en: I took the one less traveled by.
phrases.ko: 나는 사람들이 덜 간 길을 택했다. (프로스트)

phrases.en: Make your choice the right one.

response.situationKo: 인생의 갈림길에서 내린 선택을 돌아보며 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Was there a moment when you chose a road less traveled?

answers.text: When I left engineering for teaching, most people thought I was mad. Looking back, it made all the difference.
I chose a small company instead of a big brand. I learned three times as fast.
Honestly, my choices were ordinary. But I've learned to tell them as if they were brave.
Moving to a city where I knew nobody. Terrifying, then wonderful.

title: Hope is the thing with feathers
settingKo: 힘든 시기를 지나는 친구에게 에밀리 디킨슨의 시를 보내며 이야기합니다.

lines.text: I sent you that poem because the first line reminded me of you: hope is the thing with feathers.
lines.ko: 첫 줄이 너를 떠올리게 해서 그 시를 보냈어. 희망은 깃털 달린 것.

lines.text: I liked how she describes hope as a small bird that sings without ever asking for anything.
lines.ko: 희망을 아무것도 요구하지 않고 노래하는 작은 새로 묘사한 게 좋았어.

lines.text: Exactly. Even in the worst storms, it keeps singing, quietly, in the background.
lines.ko: 바로 그거야. 최악의 폭풍 속에서도 배경에서 조용히 계속 노래하잖아.

lines.text: It's a better image than 'stay positive'. It doesn't pretend the storm isn't there.
lines.ko: '긍정적으로 생각해'보다 나은 이미지야. 폭풍이 없는 척하지 않으니까.

gist.questionKo: 두 번째 사람이 시를 좋아한 이유는?

phrases.en: Hope is the thing with feathers.
It doesn't pretend the storm isn't there.

response.situationKo: 추상적인 감정(희망, 두려움 등)을 사물이나 동물로 비유해 표현해 보세요.
response.prompt: If fear were an animal, what would it be?

answers.text: Fear is a cat on your chest at night: small, heavy, and very hard to move.
A guard dog. It barks at everything, including the postman, but sometimes it's right.
I'd say a shadow, because it grows bigger the further you are from the light.
A mosquito. Tiny, annoying, and always shows up when you're trying to sleep.

title: The importance of being earnest
settingKo: 오스카 와일드의 재치 있는 대사를 현대 상황에 대입해 봅니다.

lines.text: In The Importance of Being Earnest, Algernon says the truth is rarely pure and never simple.
lines.ko: '진지함의 중요성'에서 앨저넌은 진실은 순수한 경우가 드물고 결코 단순하지 않다고 해요.

lines.text: That's basically every argument I've had with my sister about what happened at Christmas.
lines.ko: 그건 크리스마스에 무슨 일이 있었는지를 두고 언니와 했던 모든 말다툼이네요.

lines.text: Wilde loved turning clichés inside out. He takes 'the plain truth' and shows it's never plain.
lines.ko: 와일드는 상투어를 뒤집는 걸 좋아했어요. '있는 그대로의 진실'을 가져와 결코 단순하지 않다는 걸 보여 주죠.

lines.text: Which makes him funny and annoyingly wise at the same time.
lines.ko: 그래서 재밌으면서도 짜증 나게 현명하죠.

phrases.en: The truth is rarely pure and never simple.
phrases.ko: 진실은 순수한 경우가 드물고 결코 단순하지 않다. (오스카 와일드)

response.situationKo: 흔한 속담이나 상투어를 와일드처럼 비틀어 재치 있게 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Twist a well-known saying into something witty.

answers.text: The early bird catches the worm, but the second mouse gets the cheese.
Better late than never, but never late is better.
Practice makes perfect, except when you practise the wrong thing perfectly.
Honesty is the best policy, unless you're asked about someone's haircut.

title: Call me Ishmael
settingKo: 글쓰기 모임에서 유명한 첫 문장들의 힘을 이야기합니다.

lines.text: Call me Ishmael. Three words, and Melville has already made you curious about who this person is.
lines.ko: 나를 이슈메일이라 불러 다오. 세 단어만으로 멜빌은 이 사람이 누군지 궁금하게 만들어요.

lines.text: It's strange, isn't it? 'Call me' suggests that might not even be his real name.
lines.ko: 이상하죠? '불러 다오'라는 건 그게 진짜 이름이 아닐 수도 있다는 걸 암시해요.

lines.text: Exactly. A great first line raises a question the reader needs answered.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 훌륭한 첫 문장은 독자가 답을 알고 싶어지는 질문을 던져요.

lines.text: Then my opening, 'It was a sunny day', probably isn't doing much work.
lines.ko: 그럼 제 첫 문장 '화창한 날이었다'는 별로 일을 안 하고 있겠네요.

phrases.en: It raises a question the reader needs answered.
phrases.ko: 독자가 답을 알고 싶어지는 질문을 던져요.

response.situationKo: 자신의 이야기를 시작하는 궁금증을 자아내는 첫 문장을 만들어 보세요.
response.prompt: Write the first line of your autobiography.

answers.text: Nobody in my family had ever left the village, until the summer I bought a one-way ticket.
I was twenty-six the first time I said no to my father, and it changed everything.
Everyone remembers where they were that night. I was hiding in a cupboard.
Call me Min. Actually, everyone does, so that's not very mysterious.

title: Jekyll and Hyde
settingKo: 온라인과 오프라인에서 전혀 다른 사람을 지킬과 하이드에 빗대어 이야기합니다.

lines.text: In person he's the gentlest man in the office, but online he picks fights with strangers all night.
lines.ko: 직접 보면 사무실에서 가장 온화한 사람인데 온라인에선 밤새 모르는 사람이랑 싸워.

lines.text: A proper Jekyll and Hyde. Stevenson would have had a field day with social media.
lines.ko: 완전 지킬과 하이드네. 스티븐슨이 SNS를 봤으면 신나서 썼을 거야.

lines.text: What I find interesting is that Jekyll didn't create a new self; the potion just removed his restraint.
lines.ko: 흥미로운 건 지킬이 새로운 자아를 만든 게 아니라 약이 자제력을 없앤 거라는 점이야.

lines.text: Which is exactly what anonymity does. It doesn't change people, it reveals them.
lines.ko: 익명성이 딱 그렇지. 사람을 바꾸는 게 아니라 드러내는 거야.

phrases.en: It doesn't change people, it reveals them.
phrases.ko: 사람을 바꾸는 게 아니라 드러내는 거야.

response.situationKo: 문학 속 인물을 빗대어 사람이나 상황을 묘사해 보세요.
response.prompt: Describe someone you know using a famous literary character.

answers.text: My manager is a real Sherlock Holmes. She spots the one mistake on page forty.
My uncle is a bit of a Peter Pan. Fifty years old and refuses to grow up.
She reminds me of Elizabeth Bennet: sharp, proud, and quick to judge, but always fair in the end.
He's like Scrooge with money but a Santa with his time.

title: Boats against the current
settingKo: 과거를 놓지 못하는 친구와 개츠비의 마지막 문장을 이야기합니다.

lines.text: I keep checking my ex's photos. I know it's pointless, but I can't seem to stop.
lines.ko: 계속 전 애인 사진을 봐. 의미 없는 거 아는데 멈출 수가 없어.

lines.text: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Gatsby had the same problem.
lines.ko: 그렇게 우리는 물결을 거스르는 배처럼 끊임없이 과거로 떠밀려 가면서도 나아간다. 개츠비도 같은 문제가 있었지.

lines.text: And it didn't exactly end well for him.
lines.ko: 그리고 그에게 결말이 좋진 않았지.

lines.text: No. He thought he could repeat the past. You can't, but you can stop rowing backwards.
lines.ko: 그렇지. 그는 과거를 되풀이할 수 있다고 믿었어. 그건 못 해도 뒤로 노 젓는 건 멈출 수 있어.

phrases.ko: 뒤로 노 젓는 건 멈출 수 있어.

response.situationKo: 과거에 얽매인 친구를 문학적 비유로 다정하게 격려해 보세요.
response.prompt: I just can't let go of how things used to be.

answers.text: You can't rewrite the last chapter, but you get to write the next one.
The past is worth remembering, just not worth living in.
Gatsby tried to repeat the past. Let's not make that your story.
Put the oars down for a bit. Let's go do something new this weekend.

title: O Captain! My Captain!
settingKo: 은퇴하는 은사를 위한 송별사에 휘트먼의 시를 넣을지 의논합니다.

lines.text: For Mr. Hall's farewell, the students want to stand on their desks and shout 'O Captain! My Captain!'
lines.ko: 홀 선생님 송별식에 학생들이 책상 위에 서서 '오 캡틴! 마이 캡틴!'을 외치고 싶어 해요.

lines.text: It's touching, but Whitman wrote that poem as a lament for Lincoln after his assassination.
lines.ko: 감동적이지만 휘트먼은 그 시를 링컨 암살 후 애도시로 썼어요.

lines.text: So it's technically a poem about a captain who dies just as the ship reaches home.
lines.ko: 그럼 엄밀히는 배가 집에 닿는 순간 죽는 선장에 대한 시네요.

lines.text: Maybe keep the gesture but add a line that makes clear he's very much alive and retiring happily.
lines.ko: 그 행동은 살리되, 선생님이 멀쩡히 살아 행복하게 은퇴하신다는 걸 분명히 하는 한 줄을 넣으면 어때요.

response.situationKo: 고마운 선생님이나 상사에게 짧은 송별사를 해 보세요.
response.prompt: Would you like to say something to Mr. Hall before he goes?

answers.text: Thank you for believing in us before we believed in ourselves.
Because of you, I still read poetry, and I never thought I'd say that.
You taught us grammar, but mostly you taught us to be curious. We'll miss you.
Enjoy retirement, Captain. We'll take it from here.

title: Greatly exaggerated
settingKo: 회사가 망한다는 소문에 대해 대표가 트웨인의 유명한 일화를 인용합니다.

lines.text: There's a rumor online that we're shutting down next month. Should we respond?
lines.ko: 다음 달에 문 닫는다는 소문이 온라인에 돌아요. 대응해야 할까요?

lines.text: Mark Twain, when a newspaper printed his obituary, is often quoted as saying the report of his death was an exaggeration.
lines.ko: 마크 트웨인은 신문에 자기 부고가 실렸을 때 사망 보도가 과장이라고 말한 것으로 자주 인용되죠.

lines.text: So we answer with humor rather than panic?
lines.ko: 그러니까 당황하지 말고 유머로 답하자는 거죠?

lines.text: Humor, plus one hard fact: we just signed our biggest contract ever. Confidence beats a long denial.
lines.ko: 유머에 확실한 사실 하나를 더하죠. 방금 사상 최대 계약을 맺었다고. 긴 부인보다 자신감이 이겨요.

phrases.en: The report of my death was an exaggeration.
phrases.ko: 내 사망 보도는 과장이었다. (마크 트웨인 일화)

response.situationKo: 자신에 대한 잘못된 소문을 유머와 사실로 재치 있게 부정해 보세요.
response.prompt: I heard you're quitting to become a farmer!

answers.text: Rumors of my farming career have been greatly exaggerated. I can't even keep a cactus alive.
Actually, I just signed up for a pottery class. Somehow that became a farm.
The truth is less exciting: I'm moving teams, not leaving.
I wish! Who's spreading this, and can they find me a farm?

title: With malice toward none
settingKo: 합병 후 갈등이 큰 두 팀을 하나로 모으는 연설을 준비합니다.

lines.text: After the merger, half the room will feel they lost. How do I open without making it worse?
lines.ko: 합병 후 절반은 졌다고 느낄 거예요. 상황을 악화시키지 않고 어떻게 시작하죠?

lines.text: Look at Lincoln's second inaugural, at the end of the Civil War: with malice toward none, with charity for all.
lines.ko: 남북전쟁 끝무렵 링컨의 2차 취임 연설을 봐요. 누구에게도 악의 없이, 모두에게 자비를.

lines.text: He'd just won, and he chose generosity instead of victory.
lines.ko: 막 이겼는데 승리 대신 관용을 택했네요.

lines.text: Exactly. Don't celebrate the deal. Acknowledge what people lost, then describe what you'll build together.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 거래를 축하하지 말고 사람들이 잃은 걸 인정한 뒤 함께 만들 걸 말해요.

options: 잃은 것을 인정하고 함께 만들 것을 말하라

phrases.en: With malice toward none, with charity for all.

response.situationKo: 갈등 후 두 집단을 하나로 모으는 연설의 첫마디를 해 보세요.
response.prompt: You're addressing both teams for the first time. Begin.

answers.text: I know some of you feel you lost something this month, and you're right to feel that.
Both teams built something worth being proud of. Our job now is to build the next thing together.
Nobody in this room won or lost. What we build next is what will be remembered.
Let's be honest: this is awkward. So let's start by getting to know each other properly.

title: A date which will live in infamy
settingKo: 역사 수업에서 루스벨트의 연설 초안 수정 과정을 이야기합니다.

lines.text: Roosevelt's first draft said 'a date which will live in world history'. He crossed it out and wrote 'infamy'.
lines.ko: 루스벨트의 초안은 '세계 역사에 남을 날'이었는데 그걸 지우고 '치욕'이라고 썼어요.

lines.text: One word changed the whole emotional tone, from neutral to outraged.
lines.ko: 한 단어가 감정의 톤을 통째로 바꿨네요. 중립에서 분노로.

lines.text: Exactly. 'History' describes; 'infamy' judges. And it's the word everyone remembers.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. '역사'는 묘사하고 '치욕'은 판단하죠. 그리고 다들 그 단어를 기억해요.

lines.text: So in my own writing, I should hunt for the one vague word that's doing too little.
lines.ko: 그럼 제 글에서도 일을 너무 적게 하는 모호한 단어 하나를 찾아내야겠네요.

phrases.en: A date which will live in infamy.

response.situationKo: 밋밋한 문장의 단어 하나를 바꿔 더 강하게 만들어 보세요.
response.prompt: Improve this: 'The new policy had an effect on morale.'

answers.text: 'The new policy crushed morale.' 'Crushed' tells you exactly how it felt.
If it was positive: 'The new policy lifted morale overnight.'
Instead of 'had an effect on', try 'transformed'. It's specific and active.
'The policy landed like a wet sock.' Maybe too much for a report, though.

title: Give me liberty
settingKo: 토론 동아리에서 극적인 양자택일 표현의 효과와 위험을 논합니다.

lines.text: Patrick Henry's line, 'Give me liberty, or give me death', frames the choice as all or nothing.
lines.ko: 패트릭 헨리의 '자유가 아니면 죽음을'은 선택을 전부 아니면 전무로 짜요.

lines.text: That's powerful in a revolution, but in an office debate it would sound ridiculous.
lines.ko: 혁명에선 강력하지만 회사 토론에서 쓰면 우스꽝스럽게 들릴 거예요.

lines.text: Right. It's called a false dilemma when people use it to hide other options.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 다른 선택지를 숨기려고 쓰면 그걸 거짓 딜레마라고 해요.

lines.text: So I should watch for 'either we do this, or we fail' in arguments and ask what's in between.
lines.ko: 그럼 논쟁에서 '이걸 하든지 망하든지'를 주의하고 그 사이에 뭐가 있는지 물어야겠네요.

phrases.en: Give me liberty, or give me death.

response.situationKo: 상대가 거짓 딜레마로 몰아붙입니다. 다른 선택지를 제시해 보세요.
response.prompt: Either we cut prices by half, or we lose all our customers.

answers.text: Are those really the only options? What about improving service so price matters less?
That's a bit of a false choice. We could cut prices for new customers only.
There's a lot of ground in between. Alternatively, we could bundle features at the same price.
answers.noteKo: a lot of ground in between은 중간 지대예요.

answers.text: Half or nothing? Very dramatic. Let's look at the actual numbers first.

title: Ain't I a woman?
settingKo: 평등에 관한 토론 수업에서 소저너 트루스의 연설 기법을 분석합니다.

lines.text: In eighteen fifty-one, Sojourner Truth answered men who said women were too delicate for equal rights.
lines.ko: 1851년 소저너 트루스는 여성이 평등한 권리를 갖기엔 너무 연약하다고 말한 남성들에게 답했어요.

lines.text: She described her own hard labor, then asked again and again: and ain't I a woman?
lines.ko: 그녀는 자신의 고된 노동을 묘사하고 거듭 물었죠. 그런데 나는 여자가 아니란 말인가?

lines.text: She used her own life as evidence, which left their argument with nothing to stand on.
lines.ko: 자기 삶을 증거로 써서 그들의 주장이 설 자리를 없앴어요.

lines.text: Personal experience can be more powerful than statistics when the other side is talking in abstractions.
lines.ko: 상대가 추상적으로 말할 땐 개인의 경험이 통계보다 더 강력할 수 있네요.

phrases.ko: 그런데 나는 여자가 아니란 말인가? (소저너 트루스, 1851)

response.situationKo: 추상적인 주장에 자신의 구체적인 경험으로 반박해 보세요.
response.prompt: People over fifty just can't learn new technology.

answers.text: My mother learned to code at fifty-eight and now builds websites for her friends.
In my experience, our oldest colleague was the first to master the new system.
I've seen teenagers struggle and grandparents thrive. It's curiosity, not age.
Tell that to my grandad. He's better at TikTok than I am.

title: What to the slave is the Fourth of July?
settingKo: 역사 수업에서 더글러스의 독립기념일 연설이 왜 강력한지 분석합니다.

lines.text: In eighteen fifty-two, Frederick Douglass was invited to speak at a Fourth of July celebration.
lines.ko: 1852년 프레더릭 더글러스는 독립기념일 축하 행사에 연사로 초대받았어요.

lines.text: And instead of praising the holiday, he asked what it could possibly mean to a person who was enslaved.
lines.ko: 그런데 그는 축일을 칭송하는 대신 노예가 된 사람에게 그게 무슨 의미일 수 있냐고 물었죠.

lines.text: He used the audience's own values, liberty and independence, to expose their hypocrisy.
lines.ko: 청중 자신의 가치인 자유와 독립을 이용해 그들의 위선을 드러냈어요.

lines.text: That's why it's so uncomfortable to read, even now. He holds up a mirror instead of a sign.
lines.ko: 그래서 지금도 읽기가 불편하죠. 그는 팻말 대신 거울을 들어 보였어요.

phrases.en: He used the audience's own values.
He holds up a mirror instead of a sign.

response.situationKo: 상대가 중요하게 여기는 가치로 그 행동의 모순을 정중하게 짚어 보세요.
response.prompt: Our company values say we put customers first.

answers.text: If we truly put customers first, then why does it take three weeks to get a refund?
By our own values, shouldn't support be open on weekends, when most customers need it?
How does charging a cancellation fee fit with customers first? I'd like us to be consistent.
Lovely slogan. Now let's make the phone menu shorter than nine options.

title: Opening a debate
settingKo: 토론 대회에서 찬성 측 첫 발언을 준비합니다.

lines.text: The motion is that cities should make public transport free. You have two minutes to open.
lines.ko: 논제는 도시가 대중교통을 무료로 해야 한다는 거예요. 2분 안에 입론하세요.

lines.text: Should I start with the environmental argument, since that's the most obvious one?
lines.ko: 가장 당연한 환경 논거부터 시작할까요?

lines.text: Start by defining the motion on your terms, then give a roadmap: three arguments, in the order you'll make them.
lines.ko: 먼저 논제를 당신 방식으로 정의하고 로드맵을 주세요. 세 가지 논거를 말할 순서대로요.

lines.text: So: we'll show this is fairer, cleaner, and, surprisingly, cheaper for the city in the long run.
lines.ko: 그러니까: 이게 더 공정하고, 더 깨끗하고, 놀랍게도 장기적으로 도시에 더 싸다는 걸 보여 드리겠습니다.

phrases.en: Define the motion on your terms.

response.situationKo: 아래 논제로 토론 입론의 첫 30초를 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Motion: Homework should be banned in primary schools. Opening speaker, go.

answers.text: By homework, we mean compulsory work at home. Today we'll show three things: it doesn't improve learning, it widens inequality, and it steals childhood.
First, the evidence. Second, fairness. Finally, what children lose. Let's begin with the evidence.
Ladies and gentlemen, a nine-year-old's evening should belong to play, family, and sleep. Here's why.
Three reasons, two minutes, one simple idea: let kids be kids.

title: A closing argument
settingKo: 모의 재판에서 최종 변론을 연습합니다.

lines.text: In your closing, don't repeat every fact. Tell the jury the story they should remember.
lines.ko: 최종 변론에서 모든 사실을 반복하지 마세요. 배심원이 기억해야 할 이야기를 말해요.

lines.text: So I focus on the one moment that matters: the camera footage showing my client at home.
lines.ko: 그럼 중요한 한 순간에 집중할게요. 의뢰인이 집에 있는 걸 보여 주는 카메라 영상이요.

lines.text: Yes, and then turn it into a question the prosecution can't answer.
lines.ko: 네, 그리고 그걸 검찰이 답할 수 없는 질문으로 바꿔요.

lines.text: If he was home at nine, as the footage shows, how could he have been across town at nine?
lines.ko: 영상대로 9시에 집에 있었다면 어떻게 9시에 도시 반대편에 있을 수 있었겠습니까?

options: 핵심 한 순간을 답할 수 없는 질문으로

phrases.en: Tell them the story they should remember.

response.situationKo: 회의에서 자신의 제안을 마지막으로 정리하며 설득해 보세요.
response.prompt: We're almost out of time. Any final words before we vote?

answers.text: In the end, the question is simple: do we want to be first, or do we want to be safe?
Ask yourselves which option you'd defend in a year, when the results are in.
Remember one thing: every customer we spoke to asked for exactly this.
Simply put: it's cheaper, faster, and customers want it. Let's vote.

title: Pitching with a story
settingKo: 데이터만 가득한 피치를 이야기 중심으로 바꿉니다.

lines.text: Your slides are accurate, but nobody will feel anything. Who's one real person who needs this product?
lines.ko: 슬라이드는 정확한데 아무도 아무것도 못 느낄 거예요. 이 제품이 필요한 실제 인물 한 명은 누구죠?

lines.text: Rosa runs a bakery alone. She loses about two hours every night doing paperwork.
lines.ko: 로사는 혼자 빵집을 해요. 매일 밤 서류 작업에 두 시간쯤 써요.

lines.text: Start with Rosa at eleven p.m., flour on her hands, filling in a tax form. Then show the numbers.
lines.ko: 밤 11시, 손에 밀가루가 묻은 채 세금 서류를 채우는 로사로 시작하세요. 숫자는 그다음이에요.

lines.text: And end with Rosa going home at nine instead, because that's the outcome we're actually selling.
lines.ko: 그리고 대신 9시에 퇴근하는 로사로 끝내죠. 그게 우리가 실제로 파는 결과니까요.

phrases.en: That's the outcome we're actually selling.

response.situationKo: 한 사람의 이야기로 제품이나 아이디어를 소개해 보세요.
response.prompt: Pitch your app in one short story.

answers.text: Meet Daniel. He used to spend forty minutes finding parking every morning. Now he books a spot before he leaves home.
Every evening, Ana's grandmother forgot her medication. Now a gentle reminder, and a call to Ana if she misses it.
Last winter, a student told me she studied in a café just for the Wi-Fi. That's why we built free study rooms.
Picture your worst Monday. Now picture it with no inbox. That's us.

title: Writing an op-ed
settingKo: 신문 칼럼 초안을 편집자와 다듬습니다.

lines.text: Your argument doesn't appear until the fourth paragraph. Readers will have left by then.
lines.ko: 주장이 넷째 문단에서야 나와요. 그때쯤이면 독자는 떠났을 거예요.

lines.text: I wanted to build up the context first, so the argument feels earned.
lines.ko: 주장이 설득력 있게 느껴지도록 먼저 배경을 쌓고 싶었어요.

lines.text: In an op-ed, the argument goes in the first two sentences. Context supports it afterwards.
lines.ko: 칼럼에선 주장이 첫 두 문장에 와요. 배경은 그 뒤에 뒷받침하고요.

lines.text: Then I'll open with 'Our city's libraries should stay open until midnight', and justify it after.
lines.ko: 그럼 '우리 도시 도서관은 자정까지 열어야 한다'로 시작하고 근거는 뒤에 댈게요.

phrases.en: Readers will have left by then.

response.situationKo: 아래 주제로 칼럼의 첫 두 문장을 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Topic: four-day school weeks. Give me your opening.

answers.text: It's time to give our schools a four-day week. Teachers are leaving faster than we can hire them, and this is the cheapest way to keep them.
A four-day school week sounds radical. The evidence says it isn't, and here's why.
We must stop pretending that more hours in a classroom means more learning.
Kids are tired, teachers are tired, and Fridays are already half-empty. Let's make it official.

title: Writing a eulogy
settingKo: 할아버지의 추도사를 준비하며 친구에게 조언을 구합니다.

lines.text: I'm giving my grandfather's eulogy, and all I have is a list of his achievements.
lines.ko: 할아버지 추도사를 하는데 가진 거라곤 업적 목록뿐이야.

lines.text: People won't remember the list. They'll remember one small story that sounds exactly like him.
lines.ko: 사람들은 목록을 기억 못 해. 딱 할아버지 같은 작은 이야기 하나를 기억할 거야.

lines.text: He used to hide sweets in his coat pockets for the grandchildren, even when the doctor told him not to.
lines.ko: 의사가 하지 말라고 해도 손주들을 위해 코트 주머니에 사탕을 숨기곤 하셨어.

lines.text: That's it. Start there, let people smile, and the sadness will come naturally afterwards.
lines.ko: 그거야. 거기서 시작해서 사람들이 미소 짓게 하면 슬픔은 자연스럽게 따라올 거야.

phrases.en: One small story that sounds exactly like him.
phrases.ko: 딱 그분 같은 작은 이야기 하나.

response.situationKo: 소중한 사람을 작은 일화 하나로 소개하는 문장을 만들어 보세요.
response.prompt: Tell me about someone important to you, through one small story.

answers.text: My mother always left the porch light on, even after we'd all moved out. That was her way of saying come home.
I remember my first boss staying late to help me fix a mistake, then never mentioning it again.
He used to fold every receipt into a tiny paper crane. His wallet was basically an aviary.
Every Sunday, she phoned each of her five children, in order of age, without fail.

title: A graduation speech
settingKo: 졸업식 축사 초안을 다듬습니다.

lines.text: Your draft says 'follow your dreams' three times. Every graduation speech says that.
lines.ko: 초안에 '꿈을 좇아라'가 세 번 나와요. 모든 졸업 연설이 그렇게 말해요.

lines.text: What would you replace it with?
lines.ko: 그럼 뭘로 바꾸시겠어요?

lines.text: Something only you could say. What's a piece of advice you learned the hard way?
lines.ko: 당신만 할 수 있는 말이요. 힘들게 배운 조언이 뭐예요?

lines.text: That the job I was most afraid to take turned out to be the one that taught me the most.
lines.ko: 가장 두려워했던 일이 가장 많이 가르쳐 준 일이었다는 거요.

response.situationKo: 졸업생들에게 자신만의 경험에서 나온 조언 한마디를 해 보세요.
response.prompt: Give the graduates one piece of advice, in your own words.

answers.text: When I was your age, I thought asking for help looked weak. I learned the hard way that it's the fastest way to grow.
Say yes to the thing that scares you a little. Not a lot, a little.
You'll be tempted to compare your chapter two with someone's chapter twenty. Don't.
Call your parents. Wear sunscreen. Never reply to work emails at midnight.

title: A toast with a quote
settingKo: 친구의 개업식에서 명언을 인용한 건배사를 합니다.

lines.text: I want to use a quote in my toast for Lena's new bakery, but not something cheesy.
lines.ko: 레나의 빵집 개업 건배사에 명언을 쓰고 싶은데 오글거리지 않는 걸로.

lines.text: How about Franklin: well done is better than well said. It suits someone who works rather than talks.
lines.ko: 프랭클린 어때? 잘 말하는 것보다 잘하는 게 낫다. 말보다 일하는 사람한테 어울려.

lines.text: Perfect, because Lena never talked about opening a bakery. She just quietly did it.
lines.ko: 완벽해. 레나는 빵집 연다고 말한 적이 없어. 그냥 조용히 해냈거든.

lines.text: Then say that, add the quote, and raise your glass. Thirty seconds, no more.
lines.ko: 그럼 그 얘길 하고 명언을 붙이고 잔을 들어. 30초, 그 이상은 안 돼.

phrases.en: Well done is better than well said.
phrases.ko: 잘 말하는 것보다 잘하는 게 낫다. (프랭클린)

response.situationKo: 명언 하나를 넣어 짧은 건배사를 해 보세요.
response.prompt: Raise a glass for our team's first year!

answers.text: As Franklin said, well done is better than well said. So I'll keep this short: here's to a year of well done!
They say a smooth sea never made a skilled sailor. This year, we became excellent sailors. To us!
To the people who said yes when it would've been easier to say no. Cheers!
Here's to year two, with fewer fires and more cake. Cheers!

title: A persuasive letter
settingKo: 구청에 횡단보도 설치를 요청하는 편지를 다듬습니다.

lines.text: Your letter is angry, which is understandable, but officials skim angry letters.
lines.ko: 편지가 화가 나 있는데 이해는 되지만 공무원들은 화난 편지를 대충 읽어요.

lines.text: Then how do I show it's urgent without sounding furious?
lines.ko: 그럼 화나 보이지 않으면서 급하다는 걸 어떻게 보여 주죠?

lines.text: Use specifics: how many children cross there each morning, how many near misses, and what exactly you're asking for.
lines.ko: 구체적으로 쓰세요. 매일 아침 몇 명의 아이가 건너는지, 아찔한 순간이 몇 번인지, 정확히 무엇을 요청하는지.

lines.text: So: two hundred children a day, three near misses this month, and one request, a crossing by September.
lines.ko: 그러니까: 하루 200명, 이번 달 아찔한 순간 세 번, 그리고 요청 하나, 9월까지 횡단보도.

response.situationKo: 구체적인 근거와 명확한 요청으로 짧은 민원을 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Please state your request for the record.

answers.text: I'm writing to request a speed bump on Park Lane. In the last month, residents recorded twelve cars over fifty in a thirty zone.

One crossing, one deadline, two hundred kids. That's the whole request.

title: Reviewing a book
settingKo: 독서 모임 소식지에 실을 서평을 친구와 다듬습니다.

lines.text: Your review mostly summarizes the plot. Readers want to know whether they should read it, and why.
lines.ko: 서평이 대부분 줄거리 요약이야. 독자는 읽어야 할지, 왜인지 알고 싶어 해.

lines.text: I didn't want to give too much away.
lines.ko: 너무 많이 누설하고 싶지 않았어.

lines.text: Then summarize in two lines and spend the rest on your judgment: what works, what doesn't, and who it's for.
lines.ko: 그럼 두 줄로 요약하고 나머지는 네 판단에 써. 뭐가 좋고 뭐가 아쉬운지, 누구를 위한 책인지.

lines.text: Got it: gripping first half, slow middle, and perfect for anyone who loved The Secret Garden as a child.
lines.ko: 알겠어. 몰입되는 전반부, 느린 중반, 어릴 때 '비밀의 화원'을 좋아했던 사람에게 딱.

response.situationKo: 최근 읽거나 본 작품을 짧게 평가하고 누구에게 추천하는지 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Review something you read or watched recently, in thirty seconds.

answers.text: It's about a lighthouse keeper's last year. What works is the atmosphere; what doesn't is the rushed ending. Perfect for a rainy weekend.
If you liked Sherlock Holmes, you'll enjoy it, though the twist is easy to guess.
I'd recommend it to anyone starting a new job. It's funny, honest, and surprisingly practical.
Two words: unputdownable, then disappointing. Still worth it for the first half.

title: Steelmanning
settingKo: 토론 전에 상대 주장을 가장 강한 형태로 정리하는 연습을 합니다.

lines.text: Before you argue against them, state their position so well that they'd say, 'Yes, that's exactly what I mean.'
lines.ko: 반박하기 전에 상대 입장을 아주 잘 정리해서 '맞아, 딱 그 뜻이야'라고 말하게 해요.

lines.text: That's the opposite of a straw man, where you attack a weaker version.
lines.ko: 약한 버전을 공격하는 허수아비 논증의 반대네요.

lines.text: Exactly. It's called steelmanning, and it makes your rebuttal much harder to dismiss.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 스틸매닝이라고 하고, 반박을 훨씬 무시하기 어렵게 만들어요.

lines.text: Let me try: they're not against growth, they're worried we'll lose the quality that made customers loyal.
lines.ko: 해 볼게요: 그들은 성장에 반대하는 게 아니라 고객을 충성하게 만든 품질을 잃을까 걱정하는 거예요.

options: 상대 주장을 가장 강한 형태로 정리하기

response.situationKo: 반대 의견을 가장 강한 형태로 먼저 말한 뒤 자신의 입장을 말해 보세요.
response.prompt: Some people say we shouldn't use AI in schools. What's your view?

answers.text: The strongest argument against it is that students may skip the struggle that actually builds understanding. Even so, I'd still use it, with clear rules.
answers.noteKo: 상대 논리를 강하게 정리 후 입장을 밝혀요.

answers.text: If I understand the critics, they're worried about thinking, not technology. That's a fair concern, and it shapes how I'd use it.
They're right that copying answers is easier now. My answer is to change the homework, not ban the tool.
